profile.reading:
Per Flexential's own individual facility page, this building (Flexential Atlanta - Norcross) is located at 2775 Northwoods Parkway, Norcross, GA 30071. The operator publishes a footprint of 32,740 square feet and 1.8 MW of critical load UPS capacity for this specific building, with published certifications and compliance attestations including SOC 1 Type 2, SOC 2 Type 2, PCI DSS, ISO 27001, HITRUST, SSAE 18. Georgia is projected to waive about $296 million in sales and use taxes for data center equipment this year under two statewide exemption programs, one for large or hyperscale projects (adopted around 2018, modeled on a similar Virginia law) and one for bulk computer equipment purchases; the state has waived at least $163 million annually since 2022, with waivers projected to exceed $327 million by 2026, according to the Atlanta Journal-Constitution's reporting on state tax-expenditure audits. A 2022 University of Georgia audit found the hyperscale program alone cost the state $5 million in 2018, rising to a projected $57 million by 2030. Georgia is one of 10 states projected to waive nine-figure sums annually through these programs, and in 2024 the state legislature passed a bill to suspend the hyperscale exemption for review, which Governor Brian Kemp vetoed, citing concerns about undermining investment. Metro Atlanta's data center corridor spans several submarkets, including the Douglasville area west of the city (home to Flexential's two largest local buildings), and the Alpharetta/Norcross corridor in the northern suburbs.

Georgia Power's own capacity forecasts illustrate how fast data center demand has grown in the state: the utility projected needing just 400 megawatts of new capacity over seven years in 2022, a figure that jumped to 6,600 megawatts in 2023 and reached 8,500 megawatts by 2025 as data centers proliferated, according to Atlanta Tech News' reporting. In December 2025 Georgia's Public Service Commission approved 9,985 megawatts of new generation, with about 80% of it expected to serve data center demand specifically. The Commission has said data center revenue should reduce rather than increase residential electricity bills, and cited protections including quarterly reporting on new data center activity, longer contract terms with minimum billing so data centers pay for infrastructure even if they relocate, and a Georgia Power financial backstop through 2031 if expected contracts fail to materialize; critics have argued these safeguards remain insufficient and pushed for stronger disclosure and revised tax-incentive terms reflecting current market conditions rather than 2018-era assumptions.

profile.regional_context: Metro Atlanta is one of the largest US data center markets, sustained in part by Georgia's sales-tax exemptions for large data center equipment purchases, a policy that has drawn scrutiny over hundreds of millions of dollars in annual forgone state tax revenue even as it continues to attract large operators to submarkets including Douglasville, Alpharetta, and Norcross.

reading.body:
Flexential Atlanta - Norcross publishes 1.8 MW of IT capacity across 32,740 square feet of technical space, making it a compliance-oriented colocation site rather than a node for large-scale AI compute.

The power envelope is too small to support significant GPU cluster deployments. At common AI training density of 40 kW per rack, 1.8 MW supports roughly 45 racks. At colocation density of 10 kW per rack, it supports roughly 180 racks. The floor area is large relative to the power figure, which implies either low average rack density or significant white space, though published data does not confirm which.

Six certifications qualify this facility to host regulated workloads in financial services, healthcare, and retail: SOC 1 Type 2 and SOC 2 Type 2 for audited controls, PCI DSS for payment card environments, ISO 27001 for information security management, HITRUST for healthcare data, and SSAE 18 as the underlying attestation standard. Which tenants occupy the facility is not published.

Among 33 facilities mapped in Georgia, only four publish megawatt figures, with combined capacity of 66.3 MW. This campus ranks fourth among those four, contributing 1.8 MW, or roughly 2.7 percent of the state's published total. No expansion plan appears in the data.
